items.title: Gaming’s Business Model Is Broken. AI Can Fix It
items.summary: Video games need AI not just to fix the industry’s economics, but to usher in a new era of creativity.
items.content:
Since the launch of ChatGPT, video-game makers have been in a rush — not to adopt artificial intelligence, but to denounce it, stamping their games “AI-free” as if it were an ingredient label and artificially generated content was a GMO.

Generative AI has upended practices across dozens of industries, but gaming has been a surprising holdout. The sector was an early adopter of real-time online communications and digital distribution, yet AI quickly became taboo for many Western studios. November’s launch of Grand Theft Auto VI will be the biggest in gaming history, and Strauss Zelnick, chief executive officer of publisher Take-Two Interactive Software Inc., has said that generative AI has “ zero part ” in its development. Surveys indicate that studios using it are doing so quietly, with one senior Xbox manager recently saying gaming is the only industry “afraid” to talk about the technology.

Clair Obscur became an industry darling for doing so much on a shoestring budget. Photographer: IGDB, Kepler Interactive

That’s because of a vocal fan base vehemently opposed to AI and demanding disclosure that has been likened to a “scarlet letter.” The Indie Game Awards rescinded its game of the year prize for the acclaimed Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after it emerged that the title had briefly used AI-generated material. Even the Japanese developers of Palworld said they received death threats due in part to baseless suspicions that they used such assets.

That tide may finally be turning. And it can’t come soon enough. Video games need AI, not just to fix a broken business model, but to restore the medium’s creativity.

Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Epic Games Inc., maker of the wildly popular Fortnite and Unreal Engine — the software behind many of the industry’s biggest productions — recently declared his company has gone all in on AI coding. The backlash from fans was swift and severe. But the economics are hard to argue with. Premium titles, known as “AAA” in industry jargon, now have budgets in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Boston Consulting Group Inc. found that development costs for two major publishers rose between 360% and 449% between 2012 and this decade. Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, VI has a reported development budget of over $1 billion, versus an estimated $138 million for its 2013 predecessor.

Note: 2021-23 figures represent annual average.

A megahit like Grand Theft Auto can absorb that. Most in the industry can’t. Expenses are rising faster than revenues; tens of thousands of developers have been laid off in the past five years, most recently when Electronic Arts Inc. closed the storied studio BioWare. For AAA games, the “ math simply ain’t mathing ” anymore.

The damage goes beyond profit margins. Broken economics are the reason gaming has become boring. When failure is so expensive, publishers play it safe, retreating to proven franchises, which dampens creativity. The bigger the bet, the less room there is to be strange, and the result is fewer, more sanitized titles.

Sources: IMDB; Guinness World Records, analyst and industry estimates

Many of us fell in love with gaming because of the sheer variety: new genres, experiences and ideas we had never seen before. Today’s output has become predictable. Sony Group Corp.’s PlayStation 5, released in 2020, has had fewer exclusive titles in six years than the original PlayStation sometimes saw in six weeks, and most of them have been sequels. Fans’ patience is starting to wear thin. Marvel’s Wolverine was released last month to lukewarm reviews for its cookie-cutter gameplay, despite an estimated budget of $300 million.

All art creation is a gamble. But while a movie starts with a script, a game has to be perfected through trial and error, with developers reworking its gameplay loops over and over to see what works. This is costly and time-consuming. Go too weird, and the production might not work; play it too safe, and it feels derivative. Lengthy development times, which now stretch into years, have made this worse. A formula that seemed fresh when work began can feel stale by the time the game ships.

Ubisoft enters discussions to cut as many as 200 jobs at its French headquarters.

Epic Games cuts more than 1,000 jobs amid a downturn in engagement with Fortnite .

items.title: Renoir's 19th-century Paris is a video game: The Case of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Released on April 24, 2025, *Clair Obscur: Expedition 33* reimagines Belle Époque Paris, 19th-century architecture, and French painting within a fantasy universe. In 2026, the Musée d’Orsay dedicated an exhibition to the video game, drawing parallels between its imagery and the works in its collections.
items.content:
Google Discover Preferred sources Categories: Cinema, theater and TV / Disclaimer

Released on April 24, 2025, *Clair Obscur: Expedition 33* reimagines Belle Époque Paris, 19th-century architecture, and French painting within a fantasy universe. In 2026, the Musée d’Orsay dedicated an exhibition to the video game, drawing parallels between its imagery and the works in its collections.

What if the streets of 19th-century Paris , the reflections painted by Gustave Caillebotte, and the monumental sculptures of the 19th century became part of a fantasy video game? This is one of the key themes of *Clair Obscur: Expedition 33* , the role-playing game developed by the independent French studio Sandfall Interactive, which reimagines the visual culture of the Belle Époque and the relationship between Pierre-Auguste Renoir ( Limoges, 1841 – Cagnes-sur-Mer, 1919) and his wife Aline to construct its own narrative universe. This connection to art history even reached the Musée d’Orsay in Paris in June 2026, where a special exhibition compared images from the game with works housed in the Parisian museum.

Published by Kepler Interactive on April 24, 2025, for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is a turn-based role-playing game with real-time mechanics. The story takes place in Lumière, a fictional city inspired by late-19th-century Paris . But what happens in the video game? Once a year, a mysterious figure known as the Painter paints a number on a monolith: everyone who has reached that age disappears. When the number 33 appears, a group of explorers sets out on a mission to break the cycle.

In Clair Obscur, painting is not merely a source of aesthetic inspiration but plays a direct role in the narrative. In fact, the Painter determines the fate of the inhabitants through her creative act, while the game world is built around references to European architecture, sculpture, and painting. As art director Nicholas Maxson-Francombe explained to France’s Centre national du cinéma et de l’image animée , the project’s sources of inspiration include the Belle Époque, Victorian motifs, and Art Deco elements , as well as influences from theater and the circus (such as Cirque du Soleil).

The connection to the collections of the Musée d’Orsay (and beyond) allows us to identify some specific references. Lumière’s glossy streets evoke Gustave Caillebotte’s *Rue de Paris, temps de pluie* , a 1877 painting in which rain transforms the urban landscape into a system of reflections. The aerial perspective of certain settings, on the other hand , finds a counterpart in Victor Navlet’s *Vue générale de Paris, prise de l’Observatoire, en ballon *. The architecture of the Orsay station and that of the fictional Monoco station (a playable character in *Clair Obscur*) also share similarities, while the monuments and street furniture of the French capital are reimagined in fantastical forms. The Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe appear fragmented; the Wallace fountains take on a sculptural dimension, and Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux’s *Les Quatre Parties du monde* —a monumental group supporting the celestial sphere, created in 1872—is reimagined through images of fragmentation.

One particular reference concerns Renoir . In the game, Renoir is the patriarch of the Dessendre family, and his relationship with Aline echoes that between the Impressionist painter and his wife, Aline Charigot. The connection goes beyond just the name: love, joy, and grief are themes that run through both the characters’ story and a significant portion of the artist’s body of work. The reference to painting thus becomes a tool for addressing narrative and existential issues, as well as an element of the visual composition.

From June 23 to July 19, 2026, the Musée d’Orsay displayed images from the game and concept art—some of which had never been seen before—in its central nave to highlight the parallels with works from its own collections. The initiative was part of the program associated with the exhibition *Renoir et l’amour: la modernité heureuse (1865–1885) *. On June 25, the museum also organized *Orsay Live! Renoir au Clair Obscur , an evening featuring a discussion with Guillaume Broche , the game’s creative director, and Nicholas Maxson-Francombe, followed by a performance of the soundtrack with composer Lorien Testard and singer Alice Duport-Percier.

When works of art become part of a world to explore, the way we engage with them also changes. *Clair Obscur: Expedition 33* draws on images, architecture, and the evocative qualities of French painting, transforming them into a digital universe where references to art history can be discovered even by those who do not regularly visit museums. Can a video game, then, serve as a gateway to museum collections? The dialogue initiated by the Musée d’Orsay suggests that it may be worth exploring new ways to bring the public closer to the works, without sacrificing direct engagement with them.

items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 success means "all signals" point to Square Enix making a mainline turn-based JRPG, analyst says: "Just a matter of time"
items.content:
"Square Enix has left a significant chunk of JRPG players behind" by focusing on action RPGs, he suggests

(Image credit: Square Enix) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter As Final Fantasy Resonance has a strong start, and, like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, proves what an appetite JRPG fans have for turn-based games, one analyst suggests that Square Enix "knows what it's missed out on" after its "move towards more action-oriented Final Fantasy titles."

Square Enix's new turn-based, HD-2D release launched last week and quickly dethroned Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth as the series' single-player games' highest concurrent player peak on Steam. And, as you might expect, that's translated to a lot of money for Square Enix, too.

According to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott , Resonance has now sold 400k copies across PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S, bringing in $20 million in revenue. That's obviously rather a lot, and Elliott suggests it reflects what JRPG fans actually want and that Square Enix is catering to it. It's also worth keeping in mind that this doesn't include what the game made on the Nintendo Switch 2.

"Given the strong positive reaction to – and early sales of – Resonance and last year's Expedition 33 (which is tracking way better than recent Final Fantasy games), it's clear that Square Enix has left a significant chunk of JRPG players behind during their move towards more action-oriented Final Fantasy titles," he suggests.

"While Square chased more Western trends, a Western company swept in and released Expedition 33, a game JRPG fans wanted for decades and even won game of the year at The Game Awards," he continues. "Square knows this, knows what it's missed out on, and it's seen Capcom succeed on Steam with its legacy franchises where Square Enix has arguably floundered."

Final Fantasy Resonance is the second-biggest Steam launch of any turn-based RPG from Square Enix Final Fantasy Resonance is part of a "resurgence of turn-based RPGs and JRPGs," lead dev says Final Fantasy Resonance dethrones Rebirth for the series' largest Steam peak for a single-player RPG

Obviously, that isn't to say that Final Fantasy Resonance was made in response to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, as it was in the works well before Sandfall's reveal, let alone its wildly successful launch last year. However, the timing of another turn-based RPG gaining so much traction can't be ignored, and Elliott suggests that Square Enix may consider altering its strategy going forward.

"I can see Square Enix going down a new route, with many diverging paths, for Final Fantasy," he explains. "They've already outlined their plans to go fully multiplatform, smartly moving away from timed PlayStation exclusivity.

"I can also see the company balancing its MMO, high-fidelity remakes, and big-budget mainline Final Fantasy titles with more of these smaller 2D-HD original pixel games alongside the 2D-HD remakes," he continues. "There's still a gap for a turn-based JRPG big-budget Final Fantasy, though, and all the signals are pointing Square Enix in that direction. Just a matter of time, I reckon."

It's not just Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall that the analyst suggests Square Enix takes notes from, though. After a particularly stellar year with the likes of Resident Evil Requiem, Pragmata, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword – showcasing success with new IP and old favorites alike – Elliott adds: "I'd take even more cues from Capcom, if I were them."

Final Fantasy 14 devs say Evercold's new Evolved mode isn't massive power creep: "If you don't want to change, you don't have to."

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on PS5 Drops to New All-Time Low Price at Amazon With a Coupon
items.summary: Amazon has knocked Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on PS5 down to a new all-time low price, but it's only available through a coupon. After clipping it on the store page, you can buy it for $34.65 rather than $49.99.
items.content:
If 2025's Game of the Year , Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, has been on your gaming wishlist, there's no need to wait for Black Friday sales to grab it at a discount. Amazon currently has its physical PlayStation 5 copy marked down to a new all-time low price of $34.65 - 31% off its list price - which you can get by ticking the coupon box on the store page ( see it here ).

This is the only way you'll be able to see this deal price at checkout, so don't forget to check the box before adding it to your cart. The coupon is also only available for a few more days, until October 26, so the clock is ticking to pick it up at this record-low price . Additionally, it's only available for PS5 users. If you're hoping to grab it for Xbox, you'll unfortunately have to pay full price.

If you are able to take advantage of it, though, this is quite an exciting deal to have pop up before Black Friday sales kick off. It beats where we saw it during Prime Day earlier this year and in the middle of summer when it had another coupon appear at Amazon .

And yes, there's every chance it will appear in Black Friday sales as well, but why wait to find out? Being able to grab this phenomenal game for $35 right now instead is well worth it.

Full of wonderful characters, an incredible story, and beautiful music, Clair Obscur is a game you certainly won't regret adding to your library. Our 9/10 review from Michael Higham said that it, "paints itself into the pantheon of great RPGs with a brilliant combat system and a gripping, harrowing story." So if this is your first time stepping into its world, you're in for an unforgettable time.

Of course, Black Friday sales are coming up fast, so there's sure to be even more gaming deals like this one popping up soon. But if you're hoping to check out some more early deals in the meantime, Amazon's dropped a new sale on select Square Enix games that's worth having a look at as well.

Hannah Hoolihan is a freelancer who writes with the commerce team here at IGN.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Returns November 24 With Stunning New Release
items.summary: Clair Obscur fans can look forward to a new artbook release this November.
items.content:
Image via Sandfall Interactive Add CBR on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover By Emma Singer Published Oct 17, 2026, 9:20 PM EDT Emma Singer is an Anime & Gaming Editor from New York with over three years of experience writing about media for CBR. Outside of writing, Emma enjoys doing yoga and playing tennis. Sign in to your CBR account Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 won the coveted Game of the Year award of all time 2025, and it's been hailed as one of the greatest RPGs of the last decade, if not one of the best of all time. The French RPG surprised everyone by selling more than 8 million copies and earning stellar reviews, and now, the series is returning with a new artbook that's set to expand the game's world.

The upcoming art book, The Art of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , is 352 pages and includes both stunning artwork and behind-the-scenes insight into how the extraordinary game was made. It's a truly gorgeous book that's perfect for collectors, and it even comes with lithographs that are perfect for display.

Image via Simon & Schuster On November 24, 2026, Sandfall Interactive's Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 will follow in the footsteps of many other popular video game franchises by receiving its very own art book. Written by Marina Macq, published by UDON Entertainment, and distributed by Simon & Schuster, "The Art of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" is a new hardcover release, which will be available for $59.99 USD, plus tax and/or shipping.

"Dive into the fascinating video game world of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and discover the secrets behind its remarkable creation in this official artbook," the official description begins . "An unprecedented critical and commercial success, the video game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 captivated more than 3 million players just weeks after its release."

"Created to offer fans and newcomers an engaging look into the creative process behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , this exclusive large-format volume gathers, across more than 350 pages, hundreds of previously unseen documents and illustrations used in the creation of one of the most fascinating games of recent years, including environments, characters, concept art, objects, and more."

"Author Marine Macq, immersed within Sandfall Studio during development, provides a captivating and intimate account of the choices and inspirations that shaped this enchanting universe, from the first sketches to the final renders," the description continues. "To better understand what goes on behind the scenes—and the extraordinary human adventure represented by such an ambitious project—the development team candidly shares the secrets of their experience through a series of fascinating interviews"

Marine Macq is an author and editorial assistant at Pix'n Love and, in 2017, she founded GAMMA, a video game art gallery in France. Pix'n Love has directly collaborated with UDON Entertainment on "The Art of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33", which will include 352 pages of new content.

"The Art of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" will be available for purchase from Amazon, Barnes & Noble, Bam! Books-A-Million, Bookshop, Hudson Booksellers, Target, and Walmart.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available to play on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC.

items.title: Steam Deck gets "fully functional" Game Boy mod, creator shows it off with Clair Obscur Expedition 33 gameplay
items.summary: Steam Boy is now fully functional, with footage showing Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 running directly on the Game Boy-style handheld.
items.content:
Last Updated on October 14, 2026 PC Guide is reader-supported. When you buy through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Read More Table of Contents Running Clair Obscur on a Game Boy-style Steam Deck Latest tech deals. A couple of months ago, a Steam Deck modder showed off an ambitious project that involved squeezing the handheld’s hardware into a device roughly the size of a classic Game Boy. At the time, the project was still a work in progress, with one major problem left to solve: getting its custom display to actually work. Now, the creator has returned with some good news, confirming that the Steam Boy is now fully functional.

The project comes from Reddit user PhyFawkes, who originally started experimenting with the idea after realizing how small the Steam Deck’s motherboard actually is. The goal was to build a much smaller handheld while keeping as much of the original Steam Deck hardware as possible. The result is a Game Boy-sized device that uses the motherboard, battery, speakers, and face buttons from an LCD Steam Deck , along with a thumbstick, D-Pad, and trackpad.

The display was always going to be one of the biggest challenges. The Steam Boy uses a custom 1080 x 1200 AMOLED display running at 90Hz, which is actually a higher resolution than the standard Steam Deck screen. During the earlier stages of the project, the display wasn’t functional, meaning the Steam Boy could only output to an external monitor.

That problem has now been solved. In a new update, PhyFawkes confirmed that the Steam Boy is “now fully functional,” while also sharing footage of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 running directly on the handheld. The creator admitted that getting the display working took some time, but said it wasn’t nearly as impossible as some people had suggested. More technical details about how it was achieved are expected to be shared later.

PhyFawkes also confirmed that almost all of the internals remain unmodified parts taken directly from a Steam Deck. The main exceptions are the new display and the custom adapter PCB required to connect it to the Deck’s motherboard.

Cooling such powerful hardware inside a much smaller body was another challenge. The Steam Boy uses a small 30 x 7mm fan, a heatsink, and a custom 3D-printed mount. Earlier testing showed temperatures in the 70°C range while playing TUNIC, while the system reached around 90°C in Clair Obscur.

Would you buy a cheaper version of the Steam Frame that doesn’t work standalone?

Yes, as long as the price is significantly lower ($750 or less)

Abdul is a tech writer and Editor for PC Guide, specializing in all things tech, gaming, and hardware.

items.title: Expedition 33 Star Charlie Cox Officially Confirms Role in Unannounced Sega Game
items.summary: And he spent quite a bit longer recording it than he did for Clair Obscur
items.content:
Listen Thread 2 Link copied to clipboard By Austin Manchester Published Oct 9, 2026, 10:56 AM EDT Austin Manchester is a writer and editor living in New York City. At Polygon, he covers gaming and entertainment news, reviews new video games, interviews behind-the-scenes talent, and more. He enjoys discovering hidden gems and sharing them with Polygon's audience. Previously, he was the gaming editor for AIPT Comics and has written for other outlets like XDA, How-To Geek, and The List. He enjoys soulslikes, character-driven RPGs, and third-person shooters plucked straight out of the Xbox 360 era. He also likes to flex his non-video game nerdy knowledge sometimes, whether that's explaining who's who in the new Wolverine game or recommending a comic book series about a sentient sword. News And he spent quite a bit longer recording it than he did for Clair Obscur

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Add Polygon.com on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread 2 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was Daredevil: Born Again star Charlie Cox's first foray into video game voice work, and he's already finished up recording his next game. At New York Comic Con on Thursday, Cox told IGN that he'll star in an untitled upcoming game from Sega.

Cox was born in London, but his performance as the New York vigilante Matt Murdock is so convincing that the studio was surprised when he showed up for his game recording session.

"I was like, 'Hi guys, nice to meet you! How are you?' And all of them went, 'Oh, he’s English,'" Cox said. "They’d wanted [the character] to be American. But now I’ve got to do 40 hours of lines I’ve not prepared in an accent. Yeah, I think they thought I was American."

The mix-up is somewhat understandable, especially if this team at Sega hasn't played Expedition 33 yet. (They should maybe do so before the RPG leaves Xbox Game Pass .) Cox previously said his role in Expedition 33 took him around four hours to record (writer Jennifer Svedberg-Yen later said it was more like eight hours ), so based on his 40 hours spent in the booth, it sounds like he has a more central role in this Sega game.

Cox said the praise heaped on his Expedition 33 performance made him feel like a "total fraud" given how quickly he recorded his lines for Gustave. "But I'm so thrilled for the company, I'm so thrilled it did really well," he said at a convention last year . He was nominated for Best Performance at The Game Awards , but said motion-capture actor Maxence Cazorla deserved the credit. "Any nomination or any credit I get, I really have to give to him, because I believe that the performance of that character is really down to him, and my voice was just part of that process," he said.

Image: Marvel Studios Cox was at NYCC to promote Daredevil: Born Again 's third season, which will also be its last . Premiering next spring, the show will reunite Daredevil with the rest of the Defenders.

The voice actor behind Gustave has tried the early portions of the venerated RPG, he says

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Comes To Astral Ascent In New Crossover Update
items.content:
We've been patiently hoping that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 would make its way to Switch 2 ever since it consumed our every waking hour last year. Sandfall is still yet to make that happen, but in the meantime, we have a crossover with the wonderful roguelike Astral Ascent , which we can play right now.

As revealed in today's Triple-i Initiative showcase, the sublime platforming roguelike has been treated to a bunch of crossover content from the land of Lumière. This includes three brand new bosses (Golgra, the Mime and Pétank), new rooms inspired by the game, and recruitable Expedition ally summons, each of which comes with its own special skills.

Truthfully, it looks wonderful. The crossover brings Expedition 33's world into Astral Ascent's glorious pixel art, and the trailer alone was enough to bring a tear to this writer's eye.

Here's the full rundown of everything included in the update, as detailed on the Astral Ascent Steam page:

Three Exclusive Bosses Golgra, the Mime, and Pétank have invaded the Prison, each with brand-new combat mechanics built just for this crossover. - Golgra - Calm at first, but her kicks and gestral allies get brutal once her second phase kicks in. - The Mime - Hammers, nails, walls take them both down together, or they'll revive each other. - Pétank - Runs, then rains projectiles, clones, and explosions on you.

Three New Rooms Straight from the world of Expedition 33 : Lumière , the Gestral Village , and the Campfire . One appears at random before the final boss each run: pick Expedition 33 content or the Andromeda Bar, but choose fast, it won't come back this run!

Around the Campfire Recruit a member of the Expedition as a special summon, each with their own unique mechanic: - Gustave - Heals, boosts your attack, strikes with you, and charges up a devastating finisher. - Maelle - Shifts stance with your HP; hold one long enough for a powerful payoff attack. - Sciel - Draws cards : Moon for mana, Sun for direct strikes, Twilight for a big hit. - Lune - Casts elemental spells matching your build, building to a powerful finisher. - Verso - Rank rises on hit, drops on damage taken, push it high for a massive attack bonus. - Monoco - Draws a random card, each triggering a different monster summon. You'll only get one Expedition ally per run, so take your pick, and don't forget to give Esquie a hug!

All of this is available for free to everyone who has beaten Astral Ascent on Destiny Level 0. What an excuse to dive back in, eh?

Review Astral Ascent (Switch) - Probably The Best Roguelite Since Hades

items.title: Game Pass Is About To Lose Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 And Some Other Incredible Games
items.summary: The RPG sensation and more gems are leaving in October
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was one of 2025’s best games and one of the best third-party releases ever to join Game Pass day-and-date. Players have now had over a year to finish the turn-based RPG, but for any subscribers who haven’t yet taken the plunge, time is running out. The GOTY winner is leaving Game Pass on October 15.

That leaves you just under two weeks to go and complete the journey or start it from scratch. You can rush the main story to clear it in under 30 hours, but if you want to mine all of the expanded content, a completionist run will take you more than twice that. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare JRPG-inspired games that’s managed to break through in the modern era to a broader audience, in part thanks to its novel dodge and parry mechanics which inject some fresh energy into the usual turn-based grind. It’s also worth making it all the way through to hit the twist ending .

But Clair Obscur is also not the only great game leaving Game Pass this month . The full list includes:

Pacific Drive and A Plague Tale Requiem are both excellent, especially for the spooky month. The former is a sci-fi survival crafting game about navigating a zone full of strange anomalies with a haunted station wagon. The latter is about surviving a late medieval Europe infested with disease carrying rats. Donut County , on the other hand, is a light hearted puzzle game you can finish in just a few hours that is still one of my favorite indie games of all time.

items.title: 5 Best Video Games Like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: If you enjoyed Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and are looking for more games that have a similar feel or play style, here are five that should tickle your fancy.
items.content:
Sandfall Interactive Add SVG on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover One of the best video games of 2025 was "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," developed by French studio Sandfall Interactive. Among the best RPGs outside of "Final Fantasy," the game relies on turn-based combat as it weaves an engrossing epic tale with memorable characters. The story is set in a fantasy vision of France's Belle Époque as a group of adventurers set out to save their community from a mysterious villain known as the artist. With a dazzlingly original world brought to life by sharp writing and engaging gameplay, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" reminds gamers what's possible with turn-based RPGs.

Of course, "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" has worn its influences on its sleeve and there are plenty of similar turn-based RPGs worth giving a try. From the games that inspired the 2025 title to releases that have gameplay systems that resemble "Clair Obscur," we've rounded up our favorites. Many of these games are cornerstones in the industry when it comes to stellar turn-based RPGs. These are the five best video games like "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" that fans should check out next.

Nintendo Nintendo and Square formed a tight partnership during the Super Nintendo era, with acclaimed titles like "Chrono Trigger" and "Secret of Mana" coming to the console. One game during this period that feels notably similar to "Clair Obscur" is "Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars," originally released in 1996. The game has Mario join a new team of friends, including Geno and Mallow, as they battle the villainous Smithy Gang that's invading the Mushroom Kingdom. Combat unfolds from a turn-based system, but real-time elements are included to make techniques more effective when input properly.

While "Super Mario RPG" is the most playful game on this list in regard to its tonal qualities, its gameplay mechanics definitely serve as a precursor for "Clair Obscur." But the game is a bold reinvention of what a "Super Mario" title can be, further proving that Nintendo's flagship character was more than a platforming protagonist. Nintendo released a remake of "Super Mario RPG," reimagining the classic for the Switch in 2023, wisely staying faithful to the SNES source material. While the Nintendo game and "Clair Obscur" may not share that much at first glance, that combat system and its surprisingly deep world connects the two titles.

Sony Interactive Entertainment Nearly 30 years after its initial release, "The Legend of Dragoon" is among the forgotten PS1 exclusives. A medieval fantasy RPG for a console with a game library full of them, the 1999 title follows the protagonist Dart searching for the figure who murdered his parents. Dart is joined by several playable allies in the campaign who gain the ability to temporarily transform into magical beings through what's referred to as a Dragoon Spirit. The game's combat system is its most unique aspect, revolving around turn-based inputs but in a quick time event sequence to string together combos.

It's this combat system and the general aesthetics around "The Legend of Dragoon" that reminds us of "Clair Obscur" when we play it. This is augmented by the game's transformation mechanic, allowing access to different and more powerful techniques for each character. Through a prominent use of its richly rendered in-game cinematics, the game also places a strong emphasis on its narrative, adding to the stakes. While overshadowed by titles like "Final Fantasy" and "Chrono Cross" on the PS1, "The Legend of Dragoon" definitely deserves more recognition.

Square Enix Of all the "Final Fantasy" games that align with "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33," the closest the fan-favorite franchise gets is "Final Fantasy X." A title from 2001 that changed gaming forever , the story has an athlete named Tidus who is transported to the world of Spira. Teaming up with a group of adventurers, including the powerful summoner Yuna, Tidus sets out to stop the villainous Sin from destroying the world. The game's combat system returns to more traditional turn-based gameplay rather than the Active Time Battle mechanics in prior entries, which included real-time elements.

Just looking at the broader narrative, "Final Fantasy X" and "Clair Obscur: Expedition 33" both have a similar setup and stakes, albeit executed in very different ways. But the extensive party system in "Final Fantasy X" also evokes "Clair Obscur," allowing players to freely swap out members in combat. "Final Fantasy" has since largely moved away from turn-based combat, but "Final Fantasy X" still maintains its fun factor 25 years later. One of the best "Final Fantasy" games of all time , "Final Fantasy X" redefined the franchise for the 21st century.

Sega The "Persona" RPG series has been a staple for 30 years and feels bigger than ever, especially in regard to international audiences instead of only its native Japan. The best in the franchise to date is "Persona 5," originally released in 2016 for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation 4. Since then, the game received an enhanced remaster, rebranded as "Persona 5 Royal" in 2019 while significantly expanding its availability on other platforms. The game's story has its protagonist, Joker, transfer to a new high school and tap into his powers to take on shadowy supernatural threats.

"Persona 5" is an ambitious blend of RPG combat, dungeon-crawling exploration, and social simulator elements within the context of its high school setting. Somehow, all of these disparate elements come together beautifully, with its dungeon-crawling planning complementing its combat system especially well. Like "Clair Obscur," the game also has a striking menu layout that keeps players engaged with the action, never overstaying its welcome. Perfectly accessible if you've never played another game in the series, "Persona 5" is a modern RPG masterpiece.

Sega While the "Yakuza" series was initially built around real-time third-person beat'em-up gameplay, the franchise pivoted in a big way with "Yakuza: Like a Dragon." The 2020 game introduces new protagonist Ichiban Kasuga but also pivots to turn-based combat instead of the series' typical real-time brawling. The game also shifts its setting to Yokohama as Kasuga tries to make a name for himself in the world of organized crime in Japan. Kasuga can recruit parties of up to four characters to participate in these battles, mixing hard-hitting action with the series' penchant for wacky humor.

The shift to turn-based gameplay that "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" took could've turned out disastrously in lesser hands, but the game gives the whole series a fresh energy that elevates it as it solidifies its place in the current console generation. The game also incorporates quick time mechanics that help enhance the combat, keeping players engaged both defensively and offensively, like "Clair Obscur" and its own combat timing. "Yakuza: Like a Dragon" provides a boldly new direction for the long-running series.

items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

8 Million Copies Sold

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe?

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is '95 percent' made with Blueprints
items.summary: Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.
items.content:
Keep up with the latest news, interviews, talk coverage, and other game dev insights from GDC right here on Game Developer. Read More

Sticking to a nearly-vanilla version of Unreal Engine kept Sandfall Interactive on track.

Much has been made of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developer Sandfall Interactive's production process. As you've probably heard by now, the smash hit game was produced by a studio that employs fewer than 40 people, and everyone in the game industry has a hot take about what made that possible (and often ignore the hundreds of other people listed in the game's credits ).

They've been so prolific that at a GDC Festival of Gaming talk from Sandfall chief technical officer Tom Guillermin and senior gameplay programmer Florian Torres had an entire slide advising the audience not to use their presentation as a roadmap. "This is not meant to be a tutorial or like a how-to guide on how to make games," said Guillermin. "It's a retrospective on how we made Expedition 33 ."

But let's face it, when your studio's first game is such a highly-polished hit, everyone will obviously be trying to copy your homework. Developers aiming to learn about Sandfal's process swarmed Moscone West, and let out a collective murmur of shock when Guillermin and Torres described how their small team of programmers supported such an expensive-looking game—they just used a near-vanilla version of Unreal Engine.

And they didn't use Unreal Engine to write lines and lines and lines of code in C++. Expedition 33 was largely made with Unreal's Blueprints system.

According to Torres, 95 percent of the game was constructed in Blueprints.

For the uninitiated, Unreal Engine's Blueprints system is a visual scripting tool that lets developers link "nodes" together to create different gameplay elements. It's used to define object-oriented objects or classes in the game engine. For laypeople, this mean it lets developers assemble game logic by stringing together nodes of scripting logic without constantly coding in C++.

On Clair Obscur , this meant that Guillermin, Torres, and the rest of the programmers could hand off content and feature development to the studio's designers and artists, allowing them to produce and test content in the game engine with fewer roadblocks that would rely on a programmer to create code.

Unreal Engine developers use Blueprints to different degrees. The system is deeply tied into Unreal Engine's natural codebase, and if you need to modify the engine in any way, the system becomes less reliable. In fact Guillermin said that Sandfall has a very "vanilla-first" approach when it comes to using Unreal. "We take all the tools that are natively present and we push them to their to their limits so we don't have to develop bespoke tools for the features and content of the of the game," he said.

The only "modifications" they used were old-fashioned Unreal plugins like CommonUI, GeometryScripting, ALS (Advanced Locomotion System) and KawaiiPhysics (which one commentator on Bluesky described as "one guy's freeware project for doing swooshy anime hair physics.")
